scenes.animation: Zippy runs a school with one principal who tries to be in every classroom at once, spinning in circles. Neo adds class teachers to each room, and the chaos calms. A title card appears: 'Federalism'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: One principal for fifty classrooms. What could go wrong?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Everything. That's why big countries divide power between levels of government. It's called federalism.

scenes.animation: Two stacked boxes appear: top 'Government for the entire country', bottom 'Governments at the level of provinces or states'. Both send arrows down to the same citizens. Beside it, a single box labelled 'Unitary system' sends orders downward to a smaller subordinate box.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Federalism is a system of government in which power is divided between a central authority and various constituent units of the country.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Usually there is one government for the entire country, responsible for subjects of common national interest, and governments at the level of provinces or states that look after much of the day-to-day administration.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In a unitary system, there is only one level of government, or the sub-units are subordinate to the central government. The central government can pass on orders to them.

scenes.animation: A checklist unrolls with seven items ticking one by one: 'Two or more levels', 'Same citizens, own jurisdiction', 'Jurisdiction specified in Constitution', 'Fundamental provisions cannot be changed by one level alone', 'Courts act as umpire', 'Sources of revenue specified', 'Dual objectives: unity and diversity'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Key features of federalism. There are two or more levels of government. Each level governs the same citizens but has its own jurisdiction in legislation, taxation and administration.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The jurisdictions are specified in the Constitution. Fundamental provisions cannot be unilaterally changed by one level. Courts interpret the Constitution and act as umpire in disputes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Sources of revenue for each level are clearly specified. And federalism has dual objectives: to safeguard and promote the unity of the country, while accommodating regional diversity.

scenes.animation: Two routes animate on a world map. Route one: separate states USA, Switzerland and Australia walk together and join hands, labelled 'Coming together'. Route two: one large country India, with Spain and Belgium beside it, divides power into states while staying one, labelled 'Holding together'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Do all federations form the same way?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No. In coming together federations, independent states come together to form a bigger unit. The USA, Switzerland and Australia are examples. The constituent states usually have equal power.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In holding together federations, a large country divides its power between the constituent states and the national government. India, Spain and Belgium are examples. Here the central government tends to be more powerful.

scenes.animation: A 'Board Tip' sticker flashes over a two-column table: 'Coming together' versus 'Holding together'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: in holding together federations, units can have unequal powers, and some get special powers. Mention one example of each type.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a two-level government icon. Points appear: '1. Power divided between centre and units', '2. Seven key features; courts as umpire', '3. Coming together vs holding together'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: federalism divides power between a central authority and constituent units.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: the Constitution fixes each level's powers, and courts act as umpire.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: federations either come together, like the USA, or hold together, like India.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Class teachers, you're hired. Principal, sit down.

name: What Makes India a Federal Country?

scenes.animation: Zippy flips through the Indian Constitution looking for the word 'federation'. He can't find it. Neo points to a line: 'India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: The Constitution never says federation! So is India even federal?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It declares India a Union of States. Although it does not use the word federation, the Indian Union is based on the principles of federalism.

scenes.animation: A three-tier structure builds: 'Union Government', 'State Governments', then a third tier appears 'Panchayats and Municipalities'. Three large lists unroll beside them: 'Union List', 'State List', 'Concurrent List'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Constitution originally provided for a two-tier system: the Union Government and the State Governments. Later, a third tier was added in the form of Panchayats and Municipalities.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It clearly provides a three-fold distribution of legislative powers through three lists.

scenes.animation: Each list fills with icons as Neo speaks. Union List: tank, globe, bank, telephone, rupee coin. State List: police cap, shop, plough, canal. Concurrent List: school, tree, trade union flag, wedding garland, cradle. A floating box 'Residuary: computer software' lands with the Union.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Union List has subjects of national importance, such as defence, foreign affairs, banking, communications and currency. Only the Union Government can make laws on them.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The State List has subjects of state and local importance, such as police, trade, commerce, agriculture and irrigation. State Governments make laws on these.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Concurrent List includes education, forest, trade unions, marriage, adoption and succession. Both can make laws, but if they conflict, the law made by the Union Government prevails.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Subjects not in any list, like computer software, are residuary subjects. The Union Government has the power to legislate on them.

scenes.animation: A map of India shows some states with a small 'special provisions' badge, and Union Territories like Chandigarh, Lakshadweep and Delhi shaded differently. Then a heavy padlock on the Constitution needs two keys: 'Parliament: two-thirds majority in both Houses' and 'At least half of all State legislatures'. A judge's gavel sits beside it labelled 'Umpire'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Not all states have identical powers. Some enjoy a special status. Union Territories, like Chandigarh, Lakshadweep or Delhi, do not have the powers of a state; the Central Government has special powers to run them.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Changing the basic power sharing is not easy. An amendment must be passed by both Houses of Parliament with at least two-thirds majority, and then ratified by the legislatures of at least half of the total states.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The judiciary plays an important role, and in disputes about division of powers, the High Courts and the Supreme Court make a decision.

scenes.animation: A 'Board Tip' sticker lands on the three lists, highlighting 'Concurrent: Union law prevails'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: examiners love asking which list a subject belongs to, and who legislates on residuary subjects.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a three-list icon. Points appear: '1. Union of States; three tiers', '2. Union, State, Concurrent lists; residuary with Union', '3. Amendment: two-thirds of Parliament + half the states'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: India is a Union of States with three tiers of government.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: powers are divided in the Union, State and Concurrent Lists, and residuary subjects go to the Union.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: changing this needs Parliament and at least half of the state legislatures.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Computer software is residuary. So my video games are a Union matter!

scenes.animation: Zippy opens an old 1947 map of India and lays it over a present-day map. Borders shift, names change, and new states pop up like toast from a toaster.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: These two maps don't match at all! Did someone redraw India?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In a way, yes. Constitutional provisions matter, but the real success of federalism depends on how it is practised. Let's see three examples.

scenes.animation: States reshape on the map by language, with speech bubbles in different scripts. Then new states appear labelled by basis: 'Nagaland', 'Uttarakhand', 'Jharkhand' with tags 'culture, ethnicity, geography'. A caption: 'Linguistic states'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The creation of linguistic states was the first and a major test for democratic politics in our country. Many old states vanished and new states were created, so that people who spoke the same language lived in the same state.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Some states were created not on the basis of language but to recognise differences based on culture, ethnicity or geography. These include states like Nagaland, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Some leaders feared it would lead to disintegration. But experience shows it has made the country more united and made administration easier.

scenes.animation: A bookshelf labelled 'Eighth Schedule' fills with books in many scripts, 'Hindi' plus '21 others'. A banner reads 'No national language'. A pie slice shows 'Hindi: mother tongue of only about 40%'. A calendar at '1965' shows a Tamil Nadu protest; English and Hindi books then sit side by side.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Language policy was the second test. Our Constitution did not give the status of national language to any one language.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Hindi was identified as the official language. But Hindi is the mother tongue of only about 40 per cent of Indians. Besides Hindi, there are 21 other languages recognised as Scheduled Languages.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The use of English for official purposes was to stop in 1965. But many non-Hindi speaking states demanded that it continue. In Tamil Nadu, this movement took a violent form. The Central Government agreed to continue English along with Hindi.

scenes.animation: A seesaw labelled 'Centre' and 'States'. Before 1990, the Centre side is heavy with one party's flag. After 1990, many regional party flags hop on the States side and it balances, with a label 'Coalition government'. A Supreme Court gavel stamps 'No arbitrary dismissal of state governments'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The third test was Centre-State relations. For a long time, the same party ruled at the Centre and in most states, so state governments did not exercise their rights as autonomous units.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: After 1990, many regional political parties rose, and coalition governments began at the Centre. This led to a new culture of power sharing and respect for the autonomy of state governments.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: This trend was supported by a major judgement of the Supreme Court that made it difficult for the Central Government to dismiss state governments in an arbitrary manner.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a map of India icon. Points appear: '1. Linguistic states made India more united', '2. No national language; Hindi plus 21 Scheduled Languages', '3. After 1990: coalitions and more state autonomy'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: linguistic states made the country more united and administration easier.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: India has no national language; Hindi is official, with 21 other Scheduled Languages.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: after 1990, coalition governments and a Supreme Court judgement strengthened state autonomy.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Board tip: the three tests of Indian federalism are a classic five-mark question.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Maps redrawn, languages respected, seesaw balanced.

scenes.animation: A broken handpump in a village. Zippy writes a letter addressed 'Prime Minister, New Delhi' and waits, and waits, as cobwebs grow. Neo walks him to a village meeting under a banyan tree instead.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I've written to Delhi about our handpump. Any day now.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Local problems are better solved locally. When power is taken away from central and state governments and given to local government, it is called decentralisation.

scenes.animation: Two reasons appear on sticky notes: 'Local people know local problems best' and 'People participate directly in decision making'. A caption links them: 'Local government = best way to realise democracy'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: There are a large number of problems best settled at the local level. People have better knowledge of problems in their localities and know where to spend money efficiently.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Local government also lets people directly participate in decision making. This helps inculcate a habit of democratic participation.

scenes.animation: A calendar lands on '1992: Constitution amended'. Five cards build one by one: 'Regular elections to local bodies', 'Seats reserved for SC, ST and OBC', 'At least one-third positions for women', 'State Election Commission', 'States share powers and revenue'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A major step was taken in 1992, when the Constitution was amended to make the third tier more powerful and effective.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It is now constitutionally mandatory to hold regular elections to local government bodies. Seats are reserved in the elected bodies and executive heads for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: At least one-third of all positions are reserved for women. An independent State Election Commission conducts these elections. And state governments must share some powers and revenue with local bodies.

scenes.animation: A flowchart builds bottom-up for rural areas: 'Gram Sabha: all voters of the village' feeds 'Gram Panchayat, headed by sarpanch', then 'Panchayat Samiti or Block or Mandal', then 'Zilla Parishad'. A parallel urban column shows 'Municipality' and 'Municipal Corporation, headed by mayor'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Rural local government is known as Panchayati Raj. Each village, or group of villages, has a gram panchayat, a council with several members called panch and a president called sarpanch. It works under the gram sabha, which is all the voters in the village.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A few gram panchayats are grouped together to form a panchayat samiti, block or mandal. All panchayat samitis in a district together constitute the zilla parishad.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In towns there are municipalities, and big cities have municipal corporations. The political head of a municipal corporation is the mayor.

scenes.animation: A progress bar labelled 'Largest experiment in democracy' fills up. Warning signs flash beside it: 'Gram sabhas not held regularly', 'Few powers and resources'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: This new system of local government is the largest experiment in democracy conducted anywhere in the world. It has given women a real share of power.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: But gram sabhas are not held regularly, and most state governments have not transferred significant powers or adequate resources to local governments.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a banyan-tree icon. Points appear: '1. Decentralisation: power to local government', '2. 1992 amendment: elections, reservations, one-third women', '3. Gram sabha, panchayat, samiti, zilla parishad; municipalities'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: decentralisation brings power to local government.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: the 1992 amendment made regular elections mandatory and reserved at least one-third positions for women.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: board tip, learn the Panchayati Raj levels in order, from gram sabha to zilla parishad.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Handpump fixed by the gram panchayat. Delhi, you can relax.
